text:
“Ah, there we are!” said Filippo. “I went to the Grand Hôtel and came out with Uncle Roberto, who seized the opportunity to give me one of his usual sermons. We became heated; he threatened to disinherit me, and I told him I did not give a damn; apparently, Uncle’s two million have thus gone up in smoke, but I prefer my full and absolute freedom to them. That is all, Lori; you see it was not even worth mentioning.”

Loredana, having quickly freed herself from her skirt, stood dumbfounded.

“Two million!” she suddenly repeated.

“A little more, a little less,” said Filippo. “But I have never needed his money, and you know it.”

The girl tossed her clothes onto a chair and remained standing before the mirrored wardrobe....

“Because of me!” she exclaimed.

“Lori, please,” said Filippo. “It pains me when you talk like that: it is not your fault, but my relatives’. This is nothing new: do you remember that I had told you? My relatives do not understand, and arguments are of no use....”

“They want you to leave me?” Loredana pressed him.

“Of course!” Filippo replied. “Poor Uncle Roberto is merely my mother’s instrument: she makes him act and speak, and he acts and speaks, simply to have some peace.”

“They want you to leave me?” Loredana repeated. “And they want nothing else?”

“By Jove!” Filippo exclaimed, laughing. “That seems enough to me....”

“No, they might want more,” said the girl after a moment’s hesitation. “They might want you to marry.... Because, Flopi, I do not understand.... If you left me, what would you do? Would you live without mistresses and without a wife? Is that what your relatives demand?... Do they not want you to marry? Do they not have some young lady they like and are offering you?”

Filippo fell silent, astonished, and wondered how little Lori, whom he still considered scarcely more than a child, had arrived at the truth with the sole aid of logic. To conceal his embarrassment, he rose and said:

“No, no: whatever put that into your head?... Let me look at you....”

Loredana made a gesture to keep him away and insisted:

“Truly, Flopi, have they never spoken to you about marriage? Do they not want you to marry?”

“No, indeed; those are fantasies of yours!” Filippo repeated.

“Are you prepared to swear it to me?”

“I swear it to you....”

“Are you prepared to give me your word of honor?”

Filippo hesitated for a moment; but by then he could no longer turn back.

“I give you my word of honor!” he said.

The girl covered her face with her hands and burst into tears.

“What!” Filippo exclaimed in surprise. “Now you are crying? Aren’t you happy? Perhaps you do not believe me?”

She stood before him with her arms and breast bare; she wore batiste drawers that came down to her knees, gray silk stockings, and low white slippers: she looked like a dainty little Pierrot.

“So pretty,” said Filippo, “and so wicked! But aren’t you happy, I ask you again?”

Loredana managed to answer between sobs:

“Yes,” she declared, lying in her turn, “I am crying because I am happy!”

Filippo began to laugh and clasped her to his breast, lifting her off the ground.

“Come,” he said. “Come, lovely little mask, dear little viper. You are so beautiful, I love you so much....”

The young woman twined her arms around his neck, let herself be laid upon the bed, and through her tears sought the mouth of the man who lied and kissed so well....




VIII.


The winter was unusually harsh and long that year in Venice; it snowed several times, and on clear days an icy bora blew violently. Many families left the countryside ahead of time and began the season of receptions and festivities earlier than usual; by mid-November, because of the rigors of winter, fashionable life was already flourishing in all its splendor.

Filippo was gradually drawn back into it, almost without realizing it; he found his friends again and resumed the usual round of visits and habitual engagements among those familiar groups of people to which he was accustomed.

But he took the most solicitous care of Loredana. The murmuring of society and the spitefulness of his relatives had made the girl even dearer to him, and he often gave up some social entertainment to devote his time to her. He had surrounded her with luxury, procuring outfits for her in Milan, giving her jewels, covering her in silks and lace and furs, so that her beauty might have a worthy setting.

Loredana let him do as he pleased.

She had changed; a dull, profound sorrow had been gnawing at her since the day she discovered that her Flopi lied; and lied because his friendship with Giselda Fioresi must have a meaning he could not confess to her. At first, when she realized that Filippo was resuming his social habits, the young woman anxiously followed him in her thoughts; each time, she had him tell her what he had seen and what he had said; she noticed that he never uttered the name of the young Countess Fioresi, even when it could be learned from the newspapers that the young countess attended the parties and gatherings in which Filippo took part. A thousand times Loredana had been on the point of asking for explanations, and a thousand times she had restrained herself, thinking that he would lie again.

Then, little by little, she managed to master herself; she no longer wished to know, no longer asked questions. She was his mistress, who awaited him with inexpressible longing and gave herself wholly to him with infinite voluptuousness; she silenced the terrible jealousy that poisoned her heart, swallowed her tears in silence, and always appeared cheerful and smiling. It was a heroism of every day, of every hour, which Filippo did not know of and would never know of.

Even the luxury surrounding her seemed excessive to her; she put on her fur coat and slipped the precious rings onto her fingers with a certain little shiver, thinking that the name of kept woman suited her then better than ever. She did not care; the world was so unknown and so distant to her that she did not wish to concern herself with it; but her mother, the good Signora Emma, had grown worried about her.

Loredana still went to visit Mama in the little white house on the secluded small square. Every time, she was certain to encounter along the way Adolfo Gianella, her former fiancé, who lay in wait for her. He had remained strangely faithful to her through the storm of scandal and malicious gossip that had engulfed the young woman’s name. He followed her at a distance for long stretches, gazed at her with intense pleasure, and was perhaps more in love with her than in the days when she was a virgin and innocent. Adolfo had learned everything from the mouths of the curious and the idle—Loredana’s life and love—and then he had discovered the lovers’ nest and begun to loiter in that neighborhood, to gaze at those windows, to spy upon that happiness. Humble and timid, he confided his sorrows to no one and did not speak of Loredana at home, because his family hated her. He contented himself with following the girl and seeing her beautiful, flourishing, happy.
